The tools used below are documented in the IDAES reference guide:
This notebook shows how to use the Degeneracy Hunter tool which is part of the IDAES Diagnostics Toolbox features using two motivating examples:
Inspect constraint violations and bounds of a Pyomo model
Compute the Irreducible Degenerate Set (IDS) for a Pyomo model
Demonstrates the performance benefits in Ipopt from removing a single redundant constraint
Degeneracy Hunter requires a suitable MILP solver. This course example uses `appsi_highs`; SCIP is the default in the toolbox. Select an available MILP solver explicitly.

At a particular point, a selected constraint Jacobian is degenerate when its rows are linearly dependent. A duplicated equation is a simple global example; a nonlinear model can also lose rank only at special states. The simplest example of this is the case where a constraint in the model is duplicated. For example, consider the model below:

children.html: x1+x2=1x1+x2=1\begin{align*} & x_1 + x_2 = 1 \\ & x_1 + x_2 = 1 \\ \end{align*}​x1​+x2​=1x1​+x2​=1​

children.value: Notice the two equality constraints are identical and thus redundant. This means the constraint qualifications that solvers rely on (e.g.,
Linear Independence Constraint Qualification or LICQ
) do not hold which has three important implications:
Equality multipliers can be nonunique even when the primal minimizer is well defined
The linear systems used by a solver can become singular; bad scaling is a separate issue to check
Theoretical convergence properties of optimization algorithms may not hold

For a square equation-solving problem, counting equations does not establish their independence. These two written equations impose one independent relation, leaving a family of feasible points: any pair of values for
that sums to one. The duplicated equation does not further restrict that family.

In practice, degeneracies are rarely as straight-forward as a duplicated constraint. A more common occurrence is a set of linearly dependent constraints; that is a system of constraints where one constraint in the set can be formed by a linear combination of other constraints in the set. For example:

children.html: x1+x2+x3=12x1+2x2+2x3=2\begin{align*} & x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1 \\ & 2x_1 + 2x_2 + 2x_3 = 2 \\ \end{align*}​x1​+x2​+x3​=12x1​+2x2​+2x3​=2​

children.value: Here, the second constraint can be formed by multiplying the first constraint by two. Another common example of linearly dependent constraints is the combination of a set of material balances for all components in a system and an overall material balance. In this case, the overall material balances can be formed by adding all the individual component balances together. Depending on the number of components being modeled, this system of constraints can be quite large, but the end result is the same; the model effectively has one less constraint than it would appear to have.
The absolute best defense against this is to detect degenerate equations and reformulate the model to remove them; this is the purpose of Degeneracy Hunter. Let’s see it in action.

The cell below shows how to construct this model in Pyomo.

def build_example(include_redundant_constraint=True):
    """Build the test model with an optional duplicate equality."""
    m = pyo.ConcreteModel()

    m.I = pyo.Set(initialize=[i for i in range(1, 4)])

    m.x = pyo.Var(m.I, bounds=(0, 5), initialize=1.0)

    m.con1 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.x[1] + m.x[2] >= 1)
    m.con2 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.x[1] + m.x[2] + m.x[3] == 1)
    m.con3 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.x[2] - 2 * m.x[3] <= 1)
    m.con4 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.x[1] + m.x[3] >= 1)

    if include_redundant_constraint:
        m.con5 = pyo.Constraint(expr=m.x[1] + m.x[2] + m.x[3] == 1)

    m.obj = pyo.Objective(expr=sum(m.x[i] for i in m.I))

    return m


m = build_example()

children.label: Check the rank of the Jacobian of the equality constraints

children.value: One way to check for the presence of degenerate equations is to calculate the rank of the Jacobian matrix of the equality constraints. Small singular values identify numerical rank at a chosen tolerance; inspect scaling before calling them exact dependencies. In this example the duplicated rows independently establish an exact dependence.
The Diagnostics Toolbox contains a Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) toolbox which can be used to determine the number of small singular values in the Jacobian for a model as shown below.
As can be seen above, there is one singular value less than 1e-6, suggesting we have one degenerate constraint.
Next, we can use Degeneracy Hunter to identify irreducible degenerate sets; that is, a dependent set of constraint rows with no proper dependent subset.

Degeneracy Hunter first identifies candidate degenerate equations by solving a mixed integer linear program (MILP). It then iterates through the candidate equations and solves a second MILP for each to compute the irreducible degenerate set that must contain the candidate equation.

Degeneracy Hunter requires a suitable MILP solver, users can specify their solver of choice via a configuration argument. The default option is SCIP (https://scipopt.org/) which is an open-source solver.
The cell below shows how to create an instance of Degeneracy Hunter and generate a report of the irreducible degenerate sets.

# dh = dt.prepare_degeneracy_hunter() # default solver is scip
dh = dt.prepare_degeneracy_hunter(solver="appsi_highs")
dh.report_irreducible_degenerate_sets()

Historically, active-set solvers can omit dependent rows from a working system and interior-point solvers regularize their linear systems. These safeguards do not repair the model, and modern implementations have additional strategies. Do not blindly delete an equation from a zero-flow local degeneracy: doing so can discard a conservation law away from that state. Dowling and Biegler (2015),

Irreducible sets and the candidate MILP

children.label: Irreducible sets and the candidate MILP

children.value: is a dependent set of rows with no proper dependent subset (inclusion minimal). Different irreducible sets may have different sizes. A minimum-cardinality dependence is irreducible, but an arbitrary irreducible set need not be the smallest one in the whole matrix.

The original four-step workflow is: (1) select/scale Jacobian rows using the iterate and activity information; (2) QR-factorize and identify nonpivot candidate rows; (3) solve a sparse-dependence MILP for each candidate; (4) report constraint names and dependence coefficients. Trial 6a is a 15.96% decrease relative to trial 1; trial 1 is 19.00% slower relative to trial 6a. The prose on p. 813 reports 753.9 s, while the table gives the three repetitions above. These are measured results for this case, solver and initialization procedure, not a guaranteed speedup or a theorem that degeneracy always prevents an optimal termination. “High quality” includes the study’s heat-integration/complementarity requirements; it is not every solver termination.
Scaling, active bounds, and modern tools

children.label: Scaling, active bounds, and modern tools

children.value: , describe Jacobian/SVD diagnosis after scaling. Tiny singular values can indicate poor scaling, global dependence, local rank loss, or intrinsic ill-conditioning. Their

observations are context-dependent heuristics, not unit-invariant certificates: multiplying a constraint changes singular-value magnitudes without changing its feasible set. Scale variables and equations, inspect relative spectra and vectors, and test the suspected relation at meaningful states. SVD identifies combinations of rows and variables; the MILP aims for sparse named sets and its practical cost depends on the model and MILP solver.
The paper’s warning about active bounds reducing degrees of freedom concerns a

. An additional active bound is not a universal defect in an optimization problem; optimal solutions often lie on legitimate bounds. Check independence and physical purpose. A logarithm requires a strictly positive evaluation point even if its domain is represented using a nonnegative variable bound.
